interactive.title: Charging a core at 0.1 Hz
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Twelve screens cover the VLF withstand test, with Back and Continue. They show what it is for, why it runs at 0.1 Hz, how the voltage and time are set, and String B's result.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: "What VLF test voltage range applies to a 12/20 kV cable?" Three choices, in this order: "12 to 20 kV"; "18 to 30 kV"; "30 to 50 kV". Right, the second: "Still there." Then the working: "The range is 1.5 to 2.5 U0. U0 is the voltage from each core to earth, the first number in 12/20 kV. 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV, and 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV." A last line names the two slips. The 30 to 50 kV answer uses 20 kV, the voltage between cores. The 12 to 20 kV answer is the rating itself, with no overvoltage. Then come two buttons. Refresh the why goes to screen 2. Skip to the practice goes to screen 7. Wrong, the first: "That is the cable's own rating. The test goes above it, to 1.5 to 2.5 times U0." Wrong, the third: "That uses 20 kV, the voltage between cores. U0 is the voltage to earth, 12 kV. 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV, and 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV." Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. "The VLF test is a pressure test. It holds an AC overvoltage on the insulation for a set time. The IR test checked the XLPE at 5 kV d.c. This test stresses it above its working voltage. It runs before the cable is energised." Then: "Take a defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage. The small discharges inside it are partial discharges. They start an electrical tree. That is a set of fine breakdown channels that branch out through the XLPE. The tree grows until the core breaks down, during the test. Smaller defects are not affected. So a pass means the core held the voltage for the full time with no breakdown. That gives a high chance the insulation is sound. It does not prove there are no defects at all." Then: "Not every spec uses VLF. On a submarine cable rated above 36 kV, the spec may ask for an AC test at 10 to 500 Hz, from a resonant test set.[^1] The client's spec decides." The picture shows one core in long section: conductor, XLPE and screen. A void sits in the XLPE near the conductor. Fine branching lines grow from it across the XLPE towards the screen, labelled "electrical tree: grows during the test". A smaller void further along stays as it is, labelled "smaller defect: not affected". A red line says what goes wrong if the test is skipped: "Skip it, and a defect the test would have found stays in the cable. It is still there when the cable is switched on."

Screen 3, The why: 0.1 Hz. "Each core is a capacitor, as in lesson 1. Conductor and screen are the plates. String B's core is 0.528 µF. To hold an AC voltage on it, the test set fills it with charge, empties it, and fills it the other way, every cycle. That flow of charge is the charging current. The charge in each cycle is set by the capacitance and the voltage. The frequency sets how often it flows. One cycle at 0.1 Hz takes 10 s. In those 10 s, 50 Hz runs 50 × 10 = 500 cycles. So at 50 Hz the set moves the same charge 500 times as often, and the current is 500 times bigger." The top of the picture plots the voltage across one core of String B against time, from 0 to 10 s. It is always 76 kV rms, with its 107.5 kV peak marked. At 0.1 Hz one slow cycle fills the 10 s. At 1 Hz there are 10 cycles. At 10 Hz there are 100, drawn as a dense band. At 50 Hz the 500 cycles merge into a solid band, labelled "500 cycles in 10 s". Below, a bar shows the charging current on a scale up to 12.61 A, with its value written beside it. A Frequency stepper is a named control with four settings, in this order: 0.1 Hz; 1 Hz; 10 Hz; 50 Hz. It opens on 50 Hz. There are two readouts. Charging current = 2π × f × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000, shown in A from 1 A up and in mA below. Set supplies, in kVA, = 76 × the current in A. At 50 Hz: 12.61 A and 958.4 kVA. At 10 Hz: 2.52 A and 191.5 kVA. At 1 Hz: 252.13 mA and 19.16 kVA. At 0.1 Hz: 25.21 mA and 1.92 kVA. The prompt: "Step the frequency down from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz." Read: at 50 Hz one core of String B needs 12.61 A at 76 kV. The set supplies 958.4 kVA. Each step down cuts the current in proportion. At 0.1 Hz the same voltage needs 25.21 mA and 1.92 kVA. That is 500 times less, because the core goes through 500 times fewer cycles. Still: 0.1 Hz, with the 50 Hz bar kept faint beside it for scale. Under the readouts, a second paragraph: "That is the reactance at work. Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC, so dropping f from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz raises Xc 50 ÷ 0.1 = 500 times. The current is I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV, so it falls 500 times. The power the set supplies, V × I, falls with it." Each formula stays on one line.

Screen 4, The why: long cables and the set. "A VLF set is rated by the capacitance it can drive at each frequency. Take a set that drives 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz, 1.5 µF at 0.05 Hz and 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz, up to 200 kV peak. It is a practice set, modelled on a real one.[^2] Use the rating of the set in front of you. The set can only supply so much current. Halve the frequency and each microfarad takes half the current. So the same set drives twice the capacitance. A core's capacitance grows with its length. So a long cable may need a lower frequency, a lower voltage, or both. 0.1 Hz is the standard. Go lower only when the cable is too big a load for the set at 0.1 Hz. The recommended test times are for 0.1 Hz." The picture shows a bar for one core's capacitance, 0.22 µF per km × the length. Three dashed lines mark the set's rating: 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz, 1.5 µF at 0.05 Hz and 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz. String B's 2.40 km is marked on the length scale. A Cable length slider runs from 0.5 to 8.0 km in steps of 0.1 km, opening at 2.40 km. There are two readouts. Core capacitance, in µF to 3 places, = 0.22 × length. Frequency the set can use is the highest of 0.1, 0.05 and 0.02 Hz whose rating covers the core. At 0.5 km: 0.110 µF, 0.1 Hz. At 2.40 km: 0.528 µF, 0.1 Hz. At 5.0 km: 1.100 µF, 0.05 Hz. At 8.0 km: 1.760 µF, 0.02 Hz. The set reaches its 0.1 Hz rating near 3.41 km, from 0.75 ÷ 0.22. It reaches its 0.05 Hz rating near 6.82 km, from 1.5 ÷ 0.22. The prompt: "Drag the length from 2.40 km out to 8.0 km." Read: String B's 2.40 km core is 0.528 µF. That is inside the set's 0.75 µF, so it tests at 0.1 Hz. Past about 3.41 km a core is too big for the set at 0.1 Hz, so it drops to 0.05 Hz. Past about 6.82 km it drops to 0.02 Hz. At 8.0 km the core is 1.760 µF. Still: the slider at 8.0 km, with String B's 2.40 km marked. Then, under the picture: "Why not DC? Once a cable is charged, DC needs almost no current. But DC can leave space charge in XLPE. That is charge trapped in the insulation itself. This trapped charge can speed up water trees in healthy XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE.[^3] VLF reverses the polarity every cycle. That cuts the build-up. It is still a compromise. 0.1 Hz does not stress the XLPE exactly as 50 Hz will in service."

Screen 5, Check. "You test String B's core at the same 76 kV, but drop the set from 0.1 Hz to 0.05 Hz. What does the charging current do?" Choices: "It halves, to 12.61 mA"; "It doubles, to 50.42 mA"; "It stays at 25.21 mA". Right, the first: "Half the frequency doubles Xc. The current is V ÷ Xc, so it halves: 25.21 ÷ 2 = 12.61 mA. That is why the set drives twice the capacitance at 0.05 Hz." Wrong, the second: "A lower frequency gives a higher reactance, not a lower one. The core goes through half as many cycles, so it takes half the current." Wrong, the third: "The charge in each cycle stays the same, but the cycles come half as often. So the current halves."

Screen 6, Worked example. Each press shows one more line. "A new cable rated 12/20 kV, tested for installation." The prompt: "Work each line yourself first, then press Show." Line 1: "Before you start: identify, isolate, prove dead, secure and earth. Disconnect the circuit, with no monitoring equipment left on it. Restrict access at both ends. Use only the maker's test leads." Line 2: "U0 is the rated voltage from each core to earth or screen. In 12/20 kV it is the first number: U0 = 12 kV." Line 3: "Lowest level: 1.5 × U0 = 1.5 × 12 = 18.0 kV." Line 4: "Highest level: 2.5 × U0 = 2.5 × 12 = 30.0 kV. So the range is 18.0 to 30.0 kV rms. The client's spec picks the level." Line 5: "A new cable on installation: 0.1 Hz for 60 minutes.[^4] A simple withstand on aged cable would run 30 minutes." Line 6: "It passes if the core holds the voltage for the full 60 minutes with no breakdown." Line 7: "End of test: wait for the display to show discharged. Then apply the discharge stick, then the hook straight after it, then the hand earth. Earths go on core and screen at both ends, and stay on. Charge held in the XLPE can bring the voltage back for minutes or hours after the first discharge. Prove there is no voltage before anyone touches the cable." A note under the lines: "Specs differ on the range. One range in use is 1.5 to 2.5 U0.[^5] IEEE puts installation and acceptance from under 2 U0 up to 3 U0.[^6] IEEE maintenance tests run at about 75% of that. The client's spec sets the level on the job. String B is 38/66 kV, so U0 = 38 kV. For String B, 1.5 to 2.5 U0 is 57.0 to 95.0 kV." Read: on a 12/20 kV cable, U0 is 12 kV. So 1.5 to 2.5 U0 is 18.0 to 30.0 kV rms. A new cable holds the spec's level at 0.1 Hz for 60 minutes. It passes if there is no breakdown. Then discharge it in order: display, discharge stick, hook, hand earth. Earths then go on core and screen at both ends, and stay on. Still: all seven lines shown, with the note.

Screen 7, Section A, question 5 (a). The scenario panel comes first. Parts 4a and 4b carry forward: the sheath test voltage, 8.8 kV, and L2's sheath stress when it tripped, 1.45 kV/mm. Then the test is set out once: "Assume the client asks for the VLF test on all three cores, despite L2's failed sheath test. On a real job you would stop and report L2 first. String B is rated 38/66 kV. That is above 36 kV, so a real spec may ask for a resonant test. This one asks for VLF: 2 U0 as a sine wave at 0.1 Hz, for 60 minutes on each core in turn. These are practice values." The question: "(a) Determine the VLF test voltage for String B's cores." A typed answer, part 5a, in kV: 2 × 38 = 76.0 kV rms. Slips: 132.0, "That uses 66 kV, the voltage between cores. U0 is the voltage to earth, 38 kV."; 38.0, "That is U0 itself. The spec asks for 2 U0."; 107.5, "That is 76 kV as a peak. The test voltage is given in rms." After two misses, the working shows. Then: "76.0 kV rms is 2 U0, which sits inside 57.0 to 95.0 kV. Sets are rated in kV peak. Peak = rms × 1.4142. So the set must reach 76 × 1.4142 = 107.5 kV peak. The practice set's 200 kV peak covers it. On a cable rated above 35 kV, the ends may need terminations fitted to stop flashover.[^7]"

Screen 8, Section A, question 5 (b). Parts 1a and 5a carry forward: one core's capacitance, 0.528 µF, and the test voltage, 76.0 kV. "(b) Determine the charging current one core draws at 0.1 Hz." A typed answer, part 5b, in mA: 2π × 0.1 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000 = 0.02521 A = 25.21 mA. Slips: 4.01, "The 2π is missing. I = 2πfCV."; 35.66, "That uses the peak voltage. Use the rms test voltage, 76 kV."; 75.63, "That is three cores. Each core is tested on its own." After two misses, the working shows. Then: "At 76 kV the set supplies 76 × 0.02521 = 1.92 kVA."

Screen 9, Section A, question 5 (c). Parts 1a, 5a and 5b carry forward. "(c) Determine the charging current the same core would draw in a 50 Hz test at 76 kV." A typed answer, part 5c, in A: 2π × 50 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000 = 12.61 A. Slips: 2.01, "The 2π is missing. I = 2πfCV."; 6.30, "That is the core's charging current in service, at U0 = 38 kV. The test runs at 76 kV."; 25.21, "That is the 0.1 Hz current, in mA. At 50 Hz it is 500 times bigger." After two misses, the working shows. Then: "12.61 A is 500 times 25.21 mA. The set would supply 76 × 12.61 = 958.4 kVA, against 1.92 kVA at 0.1 Hz." Then String B's results: "L1 and L3 hold 76 kV for the full 60 minutes. L2 breaks down at minute 12. These are practice values. Each core is discharged and earthed after its test. Afterwards L2 reads 35 Ω from core to screen. It is the same core that had the flat PI. Its sheath would not hold either. Record it. The next job is to find where the fault is." The picture shows three bars along a 60 minute time line. L1 and L3 run the full 60 minutes, each labelled "held". L2 stops at minute 12, in red, labelled "broke down", with "35 Ω core to screen after" beside it.

Screen 10, Section B: "Explain why VLF is used rather than a 50 Hz test on a long cable." A written answer is marked against four points. Any three make a full answer. After one more go, the model answer shows.

Screen 11, Section A, changed numbers. "Another core of the same cable type runs 3.10 km. It is tested at 76 kV and 0.1 Hz. Determine its charging current." A typed answer, in mA: C = 0.22 × 3.10 = 0.682 µF, then 2π × 0.1 × 0.682 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000 = 32.57 mA. Slips: 25.21, "That is String B's 2.40 km core. Work out this core's capacitance first: 0.22 × 3.10."; 5.18, "The 2π is missing. I = 2πfCV." After two misses, the working shows. Then: "0.682 µF is inside the practice set's 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz, so 0.1 Hz still works."

Screen 12, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson.

On the screens with working, a caption says each line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value says so.

explain.text:
A VLF test holds an AC overvoltage on each core for 30 or 60 minutes. It runs at 0.1 Hz instead of 50 Hz. At that voltage, a big enough defect sparks inside. The sparks start an [[electrical tree]]. The tree grows until the core breaks down, during the test and under control. Smaller defects are not affected. So a pass gives a high chance the insulation is sound. It is not a proof.

Each core is a long capacitor. To hold an AC voltage on it, the test set fills it with charge, empties it, and fills it the other way, every cycle. That flow is the [[charging current]]. The charge in each cycle is set by the capacitance and the voltage. The frequency sets how often it flows. One cycle at 0.1 Hz takes 10 s. In that time, 50 Hz runs 500 cycles. So at 50 Hz the same charge moves 500 times as often, and the current is 500 times bigger. In the terms you know, Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC rises 500 times from 50 Hz to 0.1 Hz. So I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV falls 500 times. At 50 Hz, one core of String B at 76 kV needs 12.61 A and 958.4 kVA from the set. At 0.1 Hz it needs 25.21 mA and 1.92 kVA. These figures treat each core as a pure capacitance. They leave out the small leakage current through the XLPE.

A VLF set is rated by the capacitance it can drive at each frequency. A long cable can be too big a load at 0.1 Hz. Then it needs a lower frequency, a lower voltage, or both. Use 0.1 Hz unless the set cannot drive the cable there. DC would need almost no current once the cable is charged. But DC can leave charge trapped in XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE.[^3] The test voltage is a multiple of [[U0]], the rated voltage from core to earth. The client's spec sets the multiple.

**At 0.1 Hz a core's reactance is 500 times higher than at 50 Hz. So a test set small enough for site can hold the overvoltage long enough for a severe defect to fail during the test.**

analogy.text: Think of a power factor correction bank on a 50 Hz board. It draws a large current with almost no real load behind it. That current is charge flowing in and out of the capacitors, 50 times a second. A long cable core is a bank like that, stretched over kilometres. Slow the supply 500 times and it draws 500 times less.
analogy.breaks: A correction bank is built to take its current all day at 50 Hz. The cable is only slowed down for the test. And 0.1 Hz does not stress the XLPE exactly as 50 Hz will in service. So a VLF test is a compromise, not a copy of service.

practice.text:
- Before you start: identify, isolate, prove dead, secure and earth. Disconnect the circuit and take off any monitoring equipment. Restrict access at both ends. Use only the maker's test leads.
- Read U0 off the cable's data sheet. It is the first number of the rating, core to earth.
- Take the test voltage, frequency and time from the client's spec.
- Check the set can do it. The peak voltage is rms × 1.4142. It must sit inside the set's kV peak rating. The core's capacitance must sit inside the set's rating at the frequency you use.
- Use 0.1 Hz unless the cable is too big a load for the set there.
- On a cable rated above 35 kV, check whether the ends need terminations fitted to stop flashover.
- Hold the voltage for the full time. It passes if there is no breakdown.
- End of test: wait for the display to show discharged. Then apply the discharge stick, the hook straight after, then the hand earth. Earths go on core and screen at both ends, and stay on. Prove there is no voltage before anyone touches the cable.

**Rule of thumb:** the charging current goes with the frequency and the length. Halve the frequency and the current halves. Double the length and it doubles.

**Rule of thumb:** at 0.1 Hz, test new cable for 60 minutes on installation or acceptance. A simple withstand on aged cable runs 30 minutes.

**Worked example:** String B is 38/66 kV, 2.40 km, 0.528 µF a core. These are practice values. The spec asks for 2 U0: 2 × 38 = 76.0 kV rms. That is 107.5 kV peak. At 0.1 Hz one core draws 2π × 0.1 × 0.528 × 10⁻⁶ × 76 000 = 25.21 mA. At 50 Hz it would draw 12.61 A.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking the voltage between cores as U0: 132 kV for String B instead of 76 kV.
- Dropping the frequency when the set does not need it.
- Setting an rms test voltage against a set's peak rating without converting.
- Putting the hand earth on before the discharge stick and the hook.
- Reading a pass as proof of no defects. Smaller defects are not affected.

b1.q: Explain why VLF is used rather than a 50 Hz test on a long cable.

points.text: A long cable has a large capacitance. At 50 Hz a withstand test on it needs a very large current and power. That often makes a 50 Hz set impractical on site.
points.cite: Notes p.6; Megger, An introduction to VLF cable testing (research)

points.text: Lowering the frequency raises the cable's capacitive reactance. So the current and power fall with the frequency. At 0.1 Hz they are 500 times less than at 50 Hz, so a set you can take to site can do the test.
points.cite: Notes p.6; University of Canterbury, A comparison of VLF and 50 Hz field testing; IAEA, Medium and low voltage cable measurements (research)

points.text: VLF still holds an AC overvoltage on the insulation. A defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage grows to failure during the test.
points.cite: Notes p.7; High Voltage Inc, VLF AC withstand testing of cable (research)

points.text: DC needs little current. But it can leave space charge in XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE. VLF keeps an AC test. Its changing polarity cuts that build-up.
points.cite: University of Canterbury, A comparison of VLF and 50 Hz field testing; INMR, Overview of cable testing (research)

b1.model: A long cable is a large capacitance. At 50 Hz its reactance is low. So holding a withstand voltage on it needs a very large charging current and a lot of power. That often makes a 50 Hz set impractical on site. Lowering the frequency raises the reactance, so the current and power fall with the frequency. At 0.1 Hz they are 500 times less than at 50 Hz. So a set you can take to site can do the test. It still holds an AC overvoltage. A defect bad enough to spark at the test voltage grows to failure during the test. DC would need even less current. But it can leave space charge in XLPE. Standards now discourage DC withstand tests on XLPE. VLF keeps an alternating test. Its changing polarity cuts that build-up.

summary.for: Is the insulation sound above its working stress? Hold an AC overvoltage at 0.1 Hz for a set time, before the cable is energised.
summary.rule:
Xc = 1 ÷ 2πfC
I = V ÷ Xc = 2πfCV
Test voltage = the spec's multiple × U0
Peak = rms × 1.4142

U0: core to earth, the first number of the rating.
One range in use: 1.5 to 2.5 U0. The spec decides.
IEEE, installation and acceptance: under 2 to 3 U0. Maintenance: about 75%.
At 0.1 Hz: 60 min on new cable, 30 min for a simple withstand on aged cable.
Check the set: peak within its kV peak, core µF within its rating at your frequency.
Rated above 35 kV: ends may need terminations against flashover.
Rated above 36 kV: a spec may ask for a resonant test at 10 to 500 Hz.
Pass: no breakdown for the full time.

steps: The why: long cables and the set

applied.problem: The mistake 'Lifting the hand earth before the discharge stick and the hook' names the wrong slip: the notes' order is discharge stick, then hook, then hand earth, so the real slip is putting the hand earth on first; 'lifting' an earth means taking it off.
Same as the practice: the slip in the notes is applying the hand earth before the discharge stick and the hook, not lifting it; 'lifting' an earth means removing it, which reverses the meaning.

'A 50 Hz test is impractical on site' is absolute: the lesson itself says a spec may ask for an on-site resonant AC test at 10 to 500 Hz; the quote says the capacitive load made plain 50 Hz testing impractical for site work, so it needs narrowing.
'VLF gives an AC test without that' overstates: the research says VLF's changing polarity reduces space charge build-up, not removes it, and the lesson's own screen 4 says it only cuts that build-up.
The model answer repeats both overstatements: a 50 Hz test is not always impractical on site (resonant sets do it), and VLF reduces space charge build-up rather than avoiding it entirely.

notes.problem: The practice set's 1.5 µF at 0.05 Hz is labelled constant from source 2, but that quote gives only 0.75 µF at 0.1 Hz and 3.75 µF at 0.02 Hz; the 1.5 µF follows from the research's 'twice the load at 0.05 Hz' (same maker), which the lesson does not cite. The figure is right; its label overreaches.
